chunk_findings.detail: The new DONE test treats a scope as complete when `ddflow next` exits 2 and the scope has no `held` or `blocked` items and no claimed in-flight items. But the same rule says waves can produce parked work (“after the wave’s merges land or park”), and the spec never states that parked items count as `held` or `blocked`. Given a scope with one parked item, no ready/held/blocked items, and no in-flight claimed item, `ddflow next` can exit 2 and the agent will follow the rule to declare DONE and clear the `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` memory slot, even though the parked item still needs to be resumed. That is a wrong stop because DONE is not actually true.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md (rule 2, exit-2/DONE test)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff adds new orchestration facts to the harness descriptors (`claude.toml`, `kilo.toml`, `opencode.toml`, `vscode.toml`) but does not update the corresponding `[verified]` blocks or record a probe/source for those facts. Under [r-agent-parity], a fact is unverified until a probe or source is recorded; for example, `wait = "Bash run_in_background + ScheduleWakeup"` is asserted for Claude Code without evidence. If that capability does not exist, the emitted Claude driver will instruct the agent to wait via a nonexistent mechanism.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/claude.toml:[orchestration]

chunk_findings.detail: The new `[orchestration]` validation only checks `loop` when the key is present. Given a non-`none` orchestration table such as `[orchestration] dispatch = "task"` (no `loop`, no `none = true`), `validate_table` passes because `_membership` returns on `value is None`; the built `Orchestration` then has `loop=""`, which is not one of `ORCHESTRATION_LOOPS` and contradicts the documented contract that the loop primitive is always a background primitive. This allows an active orchestration record to be emitted with no wave-loop primitive, so the generated driver would have no background loop to run the wave.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:validate_table

chunk_findings.detail: The template requires the wave position to be persisted so that “a compaction or restart resumes AT the wave,” but the runbook never tells the agent to read `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` before starting the wave. Given a restart after a wave where the agent had already claimed items and launched background `task` children, the restarted agent begins at rule 1, calls `ddflow next`, and has no record of which items are still in flight. If those in-flight items are not surfaced as `held`/`blocked` by `ddflow next`, rule 2’s empty-scope test sees no held/blocked items and no claimed items in flight, so the agent can incorrectly declare the scope DONE and clear the slot, losing the wave position the persistence step was supposed to preserve.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-35

chunk_findings.detail: The delta instructs the orchestrator to claim every ready item before fanning them out, while also saying Kilo memory stores only the wave position and that a restart/re-run of `/ddflow-wave` “resumes at the wave” by re-reading `next`. If a compaction or restart happens after the orchestrator has claimed items but before the corresponding `task` subagents have finished, those claimed items are no longer returned by `ddflow next --json`. Example: `ddflow next --json` returns items A, B, C; the orchestrator claims A, B, C; then the background subtask is lost and `/ddflow-wave` is re-run. The restarted orchestrator reads memory for wave N, re-reads `next`, and does not see B or C because they are claimed, so it cannot fan them out or continue them. The wave is left stranded or spins waiting, contradicting the delta’s claim that restart resumes at the wave and the rule that the loop should stop only on a question/operator gate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:11-17

chunk_findings.detail: The opencode delta tells the orchestrator to “claim each ready item” and then hand the claimed items to sub-agents, while the vscode delta for the same emitted orchestration loop says the dispatched process claims its OWN item because “ddflow's exclusive lease refuses a duplicate.” Given two ready items A and B, an opencode driver following this text claims A and B in the orchestrator, spawns one sub-agent for A and one for B, and then the sub-agent for A attempts to claim A as part of running the normal item driver; the claim is refused because the orchestrator already holds the lease, so the item cannot be merged or parked and the wave stalls. The docs need to either have the orchestrator only read/fan out ready items, or explicitly describe how a claimed lease is transferred to the sub-agent.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:9 (`claim each ready item`)

chunk_findings.detail: The step-2 DONE test requires “no item you claimed is still in flight,” but the persisted `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` slot records only “the last `ddflow next` read, which items were claimed and what each merged as.” It does not record the set of in-flight `task` subagents. Concrete scenario: the orchestrator claims item I and launches a `task` child, then a compaction/restart happens before the merge. On resume, `ddflow next --json` exits 2 and reports no held/blocked items; the restored slot has no in-flight entry, so step 2 calls the scope DONE and stops while I is still being worked. That resumes after the wave rather than at it, contrary to the file’s own persistence requirement.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md step 4 / step 2

chunk_findings.detail: The stated Kilo instantiation is “Kilo session goal + task subagent,” and the previous file implemented that with “Start a session goal with the objective … and run the ddflow-orchestrator instructions.” The emitted file now says “You are the `ddflow-orchestrator` subagent … no foreground session goal.” When `/ddflow-wave bugs` reaches a ready item, the session-goal context that is supposed to spawn the per-item `task` subagents is absent, so fanout stalls or fails; the change contradicts the specified Kilo instantiation.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/command/ddflow-wave.md

chunk_findings.detail: The new `[orchestration]` parity facts are recorded in the descriptors without adding a probe or source to `[verified]`; “a fact is unverified until a probe or source is recorded,” so the parity matrix check will flag these new facts [r-agent-parity].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/harnesses/kilo.toml [orchestration] (also claude.toml/opencode.toml/vscode.toml)

chunk_findings.detail: The new subagent-file emission path adds a filesystem-layout dependency (writing `.kilo/agent/...` / other harness subagent paths into the adopted repo) but does not add or go through a port under `ddflow/adapters`. For example, adopting `kilo` with the new `[subagents].files` descriptor entry causes `_write_harness_files` to call `_write_command` and write the orchestrator file directly, so the filesystem layout cannot be faked or swapped through the adapter layer and parallel agents can collide on shared harness files. This violates [r-adapters].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt/_commands.py:_write_harness_files

chunk_findings.detail: An `[orchestration]` section is only checked for `loop` when `loop` is present; there is no check that a non-`none` orchestration section actually has a loop. For example a descriptor containing `[orchestration]` with `dispatch = "task"` and no `loop` passes `_validate_section` and produces `Orchestration(loop="")`, even though `Orchestration.loop` is documented as "one of ORCHESTRATION_LOOPS" and the record exists to describe the wave loop. This malformed value is accepted and can be emitted as an orchestration driver with an empty loop primitive.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:_validate_section

chunk_findings.detail: The vocabulary actually contains `"none"` even though the comment above it says every value is a BACKGROUND primitive and that no foreground/no-loop value exists to pick. `"none"` is not a loop primitive, and the dataclass already has a separate `none: bool` to disable the section. A descriptor with `[orchestration] loop = "none"` passes the membership check and produces a non-disabled `Orchestration` record whose `loop` names no primitive, contradicting the guarantee and allowing another route to the same empty-loop emission problem.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:ORCHESTRATION_LOOPS

chunk_findings.detail: The added "or when the scope is empty" stop condition violates the loop's own rule in the same bullet and the change's stated "stop ONLY on a question or operator gate" requirement. If `ddflow next --json` returns an empty ready set because current work is parked/awaiting CI, unit tests, or review gates while more backlog remains, this instruction makes the orchestrator exit. The loop then has no process left to re-read `next` when those gates eventually complete. The same bullet says those long gates are "waits, never stops," so an empty ready set during a wait must not terminate the wave.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md: "Stop only on a `question` or operator gate, or when the scope is empty"
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md: "Stop only on a `question` or operator gate, or when the scope is empty"

chunk_findings.detail: The new loop says “Stop only on an operator answer … or when the scope is empty.” The orchestration contract in the intent is “stop ONLY on a question or operator gate”; an empty `ddflow next --json` ready set (even with no held/blocked) should make the orchestrator wait, because future ready items can still appear from operator-added work or later dependency events. With this instruction, the background sub-agent exits as soon as the current scope is empty and never picks up those future items.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/opencode.md item 1

chunk_findings.detail: The new vscode delta says “stop only on that empty scope or a question/operator gate.” That is wrong for the same reason: when `ddflow next` reports no ready and no held/blocked after each dispatched window exits, the orchestrator must keep waiting, not stop. The required contract is stop only on a question or operator gate, so an empty current ready set causes the background orchestration surface to exit and silently drop later work.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md item 2

chunk_findings.detail: The line changes the loop’s stop condition to “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate, **or when the scope is empty**”. The stated orchestration spec is “stop ONLY on a question or operator gate”. The added empty-scope stop can fire while a long gate is pending but the current `ddflow next --json` ready set is empty; the orchestrator then exits, the long gate completes, and no agent re-reads `next`, stalling the wave indefinitely. The spec’s wait/re-read behavior requires waiting, not stopping, in that situation.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md item 1

chunk_findings.detail: The opencode delta instructs the background wave loop to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items to sub-agents.” ddflow claims are exclusive leases: this same change’s vscode delta says the dispatched process “claims its OWN item — ddflow's exclusive lease refuses a duplicate.” If the opencode orchestrator follows the text, it claims every ready item first, then each sub-agent cannot claim the item it is handed and the work stalls under a coordinator that only fans, not executes. The orchestrator must fan ready items and let each sub-agent claim its own item.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:8-10

chunk_findings.detail: The loop contract in the stated intent is “stop ONLY on a question or operator gate,” but these deltas add an independent stop condition: opencode says stop “when the scope is empty,” and vscode says stop on “that empty scope.” Example: `ddflow next` reports no ready and no held/blocked while later work may become ready without an operator gate; the emitted driver exits instead of waiting, contradicting the one-loop orchestration spec. Either the loop must stop only on question/operator gate, or the contract must not say “ONLY.”
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/opencode.md:14-15 and docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16-18

chunk_findings.detail: The test assertion `assert set(AGENT_COMMANDS) == {"claude", "kilo"}` is checking a module-level global `AGENT_COMMANDS` or a set of agents with commands in `test_implement_command.py`. However, adding `"kilo"` to this set without ensuring that other tests importing or mutating `AGENT_COMMANDS` are updated can cause intermittent test failures due to test pollution or mismatched expectations across test runs when running pytest in parallel or different orders.

chunk_findings.detail: The new DONE test treats a scope as complete when `ddflow next` exits 2 and the scope has no `held` or `blocked` items and no claimed in-flight items. chunk_findings.detail: The template requires the wave position to be persisted so that “a compaction or restart resumes AT the wave,” but the runbook never tells the agent to read `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` before starting the wave. Given a restart after a wave where the agent had already claimed items and launched background `task` children, the restarted agent begins at rule 1, calls `ddflow next`, and has no record of which items are still in flight. If those in-flight items are not surfaced as `held`/`blocked` by `ddflow next`, rule 2’s empty-scope test sees no held/blocked items and no claimed items in flight, so the agent can incorrectly declare the scope DONE and clear the slot, losing the wave position the persistence step was supposed to preserve.

chunk_findings.detail: The delta instructs the orchestrator to claim every ready item before fanning them out, while also saying Kilo memory stores only the wave position and that a restart/re-run of `/ddflow-wave` “resumes at the wave” by re-reading `next`. If a compaction or restart happens after the orchestrator has claimed items but before the corresponding `task` subagents have finished, those claimed items are no longer returned by `ddflow next --json`. Example: `ddflow next --json` returns items A, B, C; the orchestrator claims A, B, C; then the background subtask is lost and `/ddflow-wave` is re-run. The restarted orchestrator reads memory for wave N, re-reads `next`, and does not see B or C because they are claimed, so it cannot fan them out or continue them. The wave is left stranded or spins waiting, contradicting the delta’s claim that restart resumes at the wave and the rule that the loop should stop only on a question/operator gate.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/kilo-cline.md:11-17

chunk_findings.detail: The opencode delta tells the orchestrator to “claim each ready item” and then hand the claimed items to sub-agents, while the vscode delta for the same emitted orchestration loop says the dispatched process claims its OWN item because “ddflow's exclusive lease refuses a duplicate.” Given two ready items A and B, an opencode driver following this text claims A and B in the orchestrator, spawns one sub-agent for A and one for B, and then the sub-agent for A attempts to claim A as part of running the normal item driver; the claim is refused because the orchestrator already holds the lease, so the item cannot be merged or parked and the wave stalls. The docs need to either have the orchestrator only read/fan out ready items, or explicitly describe how a claimed lease is transferred to the sub-agent.

chunk_findings.detail: The step-2 DONE test requires “no item you claimed is still in flight,” but the persisted `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` slot records only “the last `ddflow next` read, which items were claimed and what each merged as.” It does not record the set of in-flight `task` subagents. Concrete scenario: the orchestrator claims item I and launches a `task` child, then a compaction/restart happens before the merge. On resume, `ddflow next --json` exits 2 and reports no held/blocked items; the restored slot has no in-flight entry, so step 2 calls the scope DONE and stops while I is still being worked. That resumes after the wave rather than at it, contrary to the file’s own persistence requirement.

The same bullet says those long gates are "waits, never stops," so an empty ready set during a wait must not terminate the wave.

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence rule still keys wave state only by the scope token (`orchestrator_wave:<scope>`), not by an invocation/run id, so two concurrent `/ddflow-wave` runs for the same scope overwrite each other's memory. For example, if an operator starts `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice, run B saves claimed/merged state for a later wave, then a lagging run A saves an older wave into the same slot; when B resumes after a compaction or restart, it loads A's stale position and may re-claim or skip items even though the spec says restart resumes AT the wave. The wording change to “runs for different scopes never share a slot” only removes the false claim; it does not make same-scope concurrent runs safe.

If two opencode wave drivers with overlapping scopes, e.g. `/ddflow-wave bugs` and `/ddflow-wave phase-1` where `phase-1` contains `bugs`, both read the same ready item from `ddflow next --json` and follow this data record, they can both dispatch the unclaimed item to sub-agents, causing duplicate implementation and conflicting merges.

chunk_findings.detail: The wave-completion test is defined only as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left”; it never says to keep the wave alive while items claimed by this orchestrator are still being implemented by background `task` children. Given `/ddflow-wave bugs` on a scope with exactly one ready item `101`, rule 2 tells the agent to claim `101` and launch a background task (lines 16-19). If the agent then re-reads `ddflow next --json` to decide whether to wait or finish, the rule’s DONE test can be satisfied because the only item is no longer ready and the text does not require outstanding claimed/in-progress items to be counted as `held`/`blocked`; line 23 then instructs “the scope is DONE — complete it” even though the task child has not merged or parked. This can stop the wave before the fanned-out work is complete, contrary to the intent’s re-read-after-merge/park and wait rules.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop tells the surface to read `ddflow next --json`, fan the ready set, and re-read `next` after each merge or park, but it never states the required empty-scope completion stop. The earlier fix added that stop to the opencode delta, but not here. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope whose last ready item has merged and whose `ddflow next --json` result has no ready and no held/blocked items, an agent following this text has no explicit rule to report completion and stop; it only has “re-read `next` after each merge or park” and “then end” for a request, so it can keep re-reading/waiting on an empty scope or stop arbitrarily.

chunk_findings.detail: The fan-out wording says “the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item” without first claiming each ready item. Given two VS Code background surfaces whose scopes overlap, for example a second window running `/ddflow-wave phase-1` and a terminal agent running `/ddflow-wave bugs` where `bugs` is part of `phase-1`, both can read the same unclaimed ready item from `ddflow next --json` and, following this wording literally, fan it to separate agents before either claim removes it from the ready set. This reintroduces the duplicate-dispatch/conflicting-merge failure that the opencode delta and the earlier confirmed findings address by requiring “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items.”

Given two VS Code background wave drivers with overlapping scopes (for example one on `phase-1` and one on `bugs` when `bugs` is inside `phase-1`), both can read the same unclaimed ready item, see it as ready, and fan it to separate window/terminal agents. chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. If B later compacts/restarts it resumes from wave 11 instead of 12, causing items to be re-processed or skipped. The fix does not answer this because it only stops asserting same-scope safety; it does not separate same-scope runs or prevent two waves on the same scope.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous fix softened the wording to “runs for different scopes never share a slot,” but the underlying defect still holds: the persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`. Two concurrent invocations of the same scope, e.g. `/ddflow-wave phase-1` launched twice, both write `orchestrator_wave:phase-1`. A lagging run A that read wave 10 can later save that old wave over run B’s newer wave 12; a compaction/restart then resumes from a stale or overwritten wave position. chunk_findings.detail: The loop says to re-read `ddflow next` after each merge/park, but the empty-scope completion test only checks that exit 2 has no ready and no held/blocked items. If one wave has two ready items, 101 and 102: the orchestrator claims both and launches background task children; task 101 merges first, triggering a re-read while task 102 is still implementing its item. At that point `ddflow next` returns nothing ready and no held/blocked (102 is neither ready nor in the stated held/blocked categories), so the orchestrator declares the scope DONE and stops while 102 is still in flight; item 102 is stranded. The completion test must wait until all task children from the current wave have merged/parked, or `ddflow next` must include in-progress claimed items in its empty-scope determination.

chunk_findings.detail: The Roo one-shot fallback instructs “claim, gate, merge” but omits the `park` alternative that the same paragraph gives for the background loop: “after the merges land (or park, in the PR flow)”. On a Roo runtime processing a PR-flow item whose long gate (ci/review) is pending, the instruction as written directs the agent to merge the item after the gate instead of parking it, which would merge an item before its gate completes. The fallback must say “claim, gate, then merge or park” (or otherwise branch on whether the item is blocked/parked).

chunk_findings.detail: The new fan-out wording says “one read of `ddflow next --json`, the ready set fanned to one window/terminal agent per ready item,” but unlike the opencode and Kilo deltas it does not instruct the orchestrator to claim each ready item before fanning it. Given two background vscode orchestrators with overlapping scopes (for example a second VS Code window and a terminal agent both running the wave loop), both can read the same ready set before either claims an item; both then fan the same unclaimed item to separate windows, and item 3 only says each subagent claims its own item, so duplicate work/lease contention occurs where the other deltas would have claimed first.

chunk_findings.detail: This background loop now re-reads `ddflow next` after each merge or park but omits the required stop condition when the scope becomes empty. On a scope whose last ready item merges, `ddflow next --json` returns no ready items and no held/blocked items; the surface is told only to re-read `next` after each merge/park, so it can keep polling an empty scope forever instead of reporting completion. The opencode delta in the same change explicitly adds “or when the scope is empty”; vscode needs the same completion stop.

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code delta says the iteration runs in the background with the operator as the exception and describes a wave loop that re-reads `next` after each merge or park, but then the same item instructs “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” On a scope with two ready items and no question, an agent following this text ends the background request after the first merge and prints a handoff; the second ready item is not driven until someone starts a new request. The delta therefore still stops at end-of-request rather than only on a question/operator gate or an empty scope, contradicting the heading and the orchestration stop contract this change is supposed to emit.

chunk_findings.detail: The updated source-of-truth loop spec defines an empty scope as “no ready, held or in-flight items”, but the Kilo instance emitted in this same change defines DONE as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left” and no claimed item in flight. The docstring omits blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) and no ready, held, or in-flight items, this record says the scope is empty and the loop should stop, while the emitted Kilo rule says it is a WAIT. Since this record is meant to be the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a driver delta generated from it can stop with blocked work still pending.

chunk_findings.detail: The new claim-before-fan wording tells the VS Code background orchestrator to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items” to another window/terminal agent, but the same delta later says that for parallelism “each claims its own item and gets its own worktree” (line 23). Given one ready item, say `101`, an orchestrator following line 13 claims `101` and then opens a terminal/window agent for `101`; the terminal agent, following the same delta, attempts to claim `101` itself. If claims are exclusive, that claim fails and the item is left claimed by the orchestrator but not worked, stalling the wave. The emitted instruction does not say that dispatched agents must skip claiming or that the orchestrator’s claim transfers to the dispatched process.

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop rule says the background wave stops only when the scope is empty (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight) or on an “operator answer,” but it omits the required stop on an unanswered `question` or operator gate. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope with one ready item that, when claimed/fanned, raises a `question` (or is parked at an operator gate), the scope is not empty and no operator answer has arrived yet, so the literal rule tells the driver not to stop; it will keep waiting/re-reading or continuing instead of stopping and surfacing the question/gate. This contradicts the intended loop (“stop ONLY on a question or operator gate”) and the kilo-cline delta in the same diff, which says “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate.”

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence slot is still keyed only by `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, and the added text “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” is only an instruction, not an enforcement mechanism: no run/invocation id, lock, or active-run marker is specified for a second orchestrator to check. If an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice from two terminals, run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 over it. A later compaction/restart resumes from the stale wave. The prior fix does not answer this interleaving because both runs are already concurrent and neither has a way to detect the other before writing the same key.

A generator transcribing this docstring will emit a stop rule that treats a blocked item—e.g. an item waiting on a lease/dependency that will later become ready—as not preventing completion, so the driver stops while the scope is not empty and skips that item.

Given a ready item that raises an operator gate/question and then waits, an agent following this line sees no operator answer yet and therefore does not treat the pending gate as the stop; it may keep re-reading/polling instead of waiting for the operator. chunk_findings.detail: The new sentence claims the claim lease enforces "one run per scope, so the slot is never written by two runs", but a claim lease guards *claims*, not writes to the memory slot `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, which is still keyed only by the scope token. Demonstrating input: `/ddflow-wave bugs` is started twice; run A claims item 101, launches its task child, and stalls before persisting; run B then reads `ddflow next`, finds item 102 still unleased, claims it (the lease never fires, because A and B claimed disjoint items), and persists the newer wave position into `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; when A's child merges 101, A persists its older wave position over B's. A later compaction or restart of run B loads A's stale position and loses track of 102's in-flight/merged status. The lease therefore does not make the "never written by two runs" claim true, and the earlier confirmed defect (persistence keyed only by scope, with no run/invocation id or slot lock) still stands at this new wording; the change also gives no instruction telling a second run to stop when its claims fail, while rule 5 says stop happens only on DONE or a question, so the losing run keeps driving and keeps writing the shared slot.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36-37 (and the identical text at ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:35-36)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop still gives the orchestrating request a direct claim step: “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge”. That contradicts the immediately preceding sentence, which says the fan-out dispatches each ready item to a window/terminal agent that “claims its OWN item”. Given one ready item `101`, a background VS Code surface following this paragraph fans `101` to a terminal agent (which will claim `101`) and then follows the “claim” instruction itself; ddflow’s exclusive lease then refuses one of the two claims, so either the child cannot start or the background contends, and the wave can stall or skip that item. The delta should say the dispatched processes claim/gate/merge while the background only waits and re-reads. The same text is in `docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18`.

chunk_findings.detail: The added “enforcement” does not make the persistence slot single-writer. ddflow’s claim lease is item-scoped — the text itself says “those items already leased” — not a run/scope mutex. Given a scope with two ready items 101 and 102, run A can claim 101 and pause before saving, while run B (`/ddflow-wave bugs`) starts, claims 102, and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; then A saves its older read over B’s slot. A later compaction/restart resumes from whichever write landed last, not necessarily the newest wave. This is the previous persistence-overwrite defect still present; the claim-lease fix does not answer it because it only stops duplicate per-item claims, not concurrent same-scope runs writing the same memory key.

chunk_findings.detail: The empty-scope stop test is `empty scope (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight)`, but the new dispatch model tells the background surface to fan each ready item WITHOUT claiming it (lines 13-14) and then re-read only `ddflow next --json`. `ddflow next` does not list an item that has been claimed and is still being implemented; the matching Kilo loop in this same change requires a separate “no item you claimed is still in flight” test for exactly that reason. Because the vscode surface did not claim the items and is given no instruction to wait for or track the spawned window/terminal agents, it cannot evaluate “none in flight.” Concrete input: ready items 101 and 102 are fanned to two agents; 102 merges first. The surface re-reads `ddflow next --json` and sees no ready and no held/blocked (101 is claimed/unreported). It can declare the scope empty and stop/hand off while 101 is still being implemented, so the loop stops before all in-flight work has finished.

chunk_findings.detail: The new ownership rule persists “your own agent/session id” and tells the agent to stop if, on resume, the stored id is not the current one, but it never clears the slot on a normal stop or checks whether the stored owner is still alive. This makes a completed or crashed run permanently own the scope. For example, run A starts `/ddflow-wave bugs`, saves session id `s1`, then crashes; a later Kilo session starts as `s2`, loads `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, sees `s1 != s2`, and follows rule 4 by stopping instead of resuming or starting, even though no run owns the scope. The same text is shipped in `.kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md`, so the emitted agent inherits the failure.

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope stop defines completion as `ddflow next` reporting “no ready and no held/blocked” and then asserts “an in-flight item is held by its lease.” That assertion is not how the corrected wave loop semantics work: a claimed/in-flight item is not reported as `held`/`blocked` by `ddflow next`, which is why the Kilo wave rule requires a separate “no item you claimed is still in flight” check. Given a scope with one ready item `101`, the background request fans `101` to a terminal/window agent, that agent claims it and is still implementing it. A re-read of `ddflow next --json` now returns no ready and no held/blocked items, so this text tells the VS Code driver that the scope is empty and the request may stop and print the handoff while `101` is still in flight, prematurely ending the wave and leaving no driver waiting for the merge/park.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The new ownership token is checked only “On resume, if the stored id is not yours,” not when a fresh `/ddflow-wave` run starts. A brand-new run never reads the existing `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` before claiming or saving, so two concurrent same-scope runs can still overwrite each other’s wave position. Concrete interleaving: an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` from two terminals. Run A saves wave 10 with id A; run B starts fresh, sees no resume condition, claims items, and saves wave 12 with id B, overwriting A. Run A then saves wave 11 over B. A later compaction or restart resumes from whichever write landed last, potentially re-claiming or skipping items. The stated “one `/ddflow-wave` run per scope at a time” is therefore still not enforced for concurrent fresh starts.

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope condition asserts that “an in-flight item is held by its lease,” so it defines empty solely as `ddflow next` reporting no ready and no held/blocked. But this VS Code driver has the background surface fan each ready item to a child process that claims its own item, and the surface keeps no separate record of which children are still implementing. `ddflow next` after a claim does not show the claimed, still-in-flight item as held/blocked — the Kilo loop in this same change had to add an explicit “no item you claimed is still in flight” check for exactly that reason. Concrete failure: with one ready item `101`, the surface fans `101` to a terminal agent, which claims it and starts the gates/merge; the surface re-reads `ddflow next`, sees no ready and no held/blocked, and, following this line, treats the scope as empty and stops/hands off before `101` completes. The stop condition must test for no fanned/claimed item still in flight, not infer that state from `ddflow next`’s held/blocked categories.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten stop condition defines completion as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited … and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” but it no longer requires that there be no held or blocked items. Given a VS Code background wave on a scope with ready item `101` and blocked item `102` (for example, `102` waiting on an unmet dependency), the driver fans `101`; after `101` merges and its child exits, `ddflow next --json` reports no ready items. Following line 17 literally, the driver treats that as the empty scope and stops, even though `102` remains blocked and the scope is not DONE. The corrected wave loop requires no ready, held, blocked, or in-flight items before stopping, so this delta can abandon remaining work.

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code wave stop condition defines completion as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited (merged or parked) and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” dropping the previous “no held/blocked” part of the empty-scope test. Since `ddflow next` only reports ready work, a scope with no ready or in-flight items but one blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) satisfies this literal rule, so a background VS Code driver can stop and treat the scope as complete while blocked work remains; the corrected wave DONE test used elsewhere in this change requires no held or blocked items left.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten vscode empty-scope stop condition now says to stop when all dispatched windows/terminals have exited and `ddflow next` reports “nothing ready,” but it no longer requires `ddflow next` to report no held/blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a held or blocked item (for example an item `ddflow park`ed waiting on a long gate, or blocked on an unmet dependency), `ddflow next --json` reports that item as held/blocked rather than ready, and no dispatched window is running; an agent following this text treats the scope as empty and stops, leaving the held/blocked item unprocessed. The previous wording explicitly included “no ready and no held/blocked”; the new wording drops the held/blocked half of the completion test.

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope stop condition is defined as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited (merged or parked) and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” but it omits held/blocked items. The loop’s empty-scope condition must be no ready and no held/blocked items (plus no in-flight), as the rest of this change requires.

chunk_findings.detail: The loop says to re-read `ddflow next` after each merge/park, but the empty-scope completion test only checks that exit 2 has no ready and no held/blocked items. If one wave has two ready items, 101 and 102: the orchestrator claims both and launches background task children; task 101 merges first, triggering a re-read while task 102 is still implementing its item. At that point `ddflow next` returns nothing ready and no held/blocked (102 is neither ready nor in the stated held/blocked categories), so the orchestrator declares the scope DONE and stops while 102 is still in flight; item 102 is stranded. chunk_findings.detail: The updated source-of-truth loop spec defines an empty scope as “no ready, held or in-flight items”, but the Kilo instance emitted in this same change defines DONE as `ddflow next` exit 2 plus “no held or blocked items left” and no claimed item in flight. The docstring omits blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) and no ready, held, or in-flight items, this record says the scope is empty and the loop should stop, while the emitted Kilo rule says it is a WAIT. Since this record is meant to be the harness-agnostic data emitted per harness, a driver delta generated from it can stop with blocked work still pending.

chunk_findings.detail: The new claim-before-fan wording tells the VS Code background orchestrator to “claim each ready item, then fan the claimed items” to another window/terminal agent, but the same delta later says that for parallelism “each claims its own item and gets its own worktree” (line 23). Given one ready item, say `101`, an orchestrator following line 13 claims `101` and then opens a terminal/window agent for `101`; the terminal agent, following the same delta, attempts to claim `101` itself. If claims are exclusive, that claim fails and the item is left claimed by the orchestrator but not worked, stalling the wave. The emitted instruction does not say that dispatched agents must skip claiming or that the orchestrator’s claim transfers to the dispatched process.

chunk_findings.detail: The new stop rule says the background wave stops only when the scope is empty (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight) or on an “operator answer,” but it omits the required stop on an unanswered `question` or operator gate. Given a VS Code background surface driving a scope with one ready item that, when claimed/fanned, raises a `question` (or is parked at an operator gate), the scope is not empty and no operator answer has arrived yet, so the literal rule tells the driver not to stop; it will keep waiting/re-reading or continuing instead of stopping and surfacing the question/gate. This contradicts the intended loop (“stop ONLY on a question or operator gate”) and the kilo-cline delta in the same diff, which says “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate.”

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence slot is still keyed only by `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, and the added text “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” is only an instruction, not an enforcement mechanism: no run/invocation id, lock, or active-run marker is specified for a second orchestrator to check. If an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` twice from two terminals, run A reads wave 10 and stalls before saving, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 over it. A later compaction/restart resumes from the stale wave. The prior fix does not answer this interleaving because both runs are already concurrent and neither has a way to detect the other before writing the same key.

chunk_findings.detail: The persistence key is still only `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` with no run/invocation id. The new sentence “Do not run the same scope twice concurrently” does not tell the agent how to detect an existing same-scope run or refuse to start, and there is no lock on the memory slot. The prior interleaving still occurs as soon as that instruction is violated: run A reads wave 10 and stalls, run B reads wave 12 and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, then run A saves wave 11 and overwrites B; a later compaction or restart resumes from the stale position and can re-claim or skip items. A generator transcribing this docstring will emit a stop rule that treats a blocked item—e.g. an item waiting on a lease/dependency that will later become ready—as not preventing completion, so the driver stops while the scope is not empty and skips that item.

The two instructions contradict for the same VS Code driver.

chunk_findings.detail: The paragraph says “Stop only on the empty scope … or an operator answer. Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge — then end with `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` output.” For a scope with two ready items, after the first merge the empty-scope stop condition is false (the second item is still ready/in flight), so the “then end” instruction causes a premature handoff instead of re-reading `ddflow next` after each merge until the scope is actually empty. The rewrite did not remove this conflict.

chunk_findings.detail: The stop condition says “Stop only on the empty scope … or an operator answer,” but the correct loop stop is on a `question` or operator gate, not on the answer. Given a ready item that raises an operator gate/question and then waits, an agent following this line sees no operator answer yet and therefore does not treat the pending gate as the stop; it may keep re-reading/polling instead of waiting for the operator. The neighboring kilo-cline delta uses the correct “Stop only on a `question` or operator gate” wording.

chunk_findings.detail: The handoff instruction still writes `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence` with underscores, while the current kilo-cline delta says `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` and the actual commands use a space. An agent executing the VS Code delta literally prints invalid command names, breaking the handoff.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentence claims the claim lease enforces "one run per scope, so the slot is never written by two runs", but a claim lease guards *claims*, not writes to the memory slot `orchestrator_wave:<scope>`, which is still keyed only by the scope token. Demonstrating input: `/ddflow-wave bugs` is started twice; run A claims item 101, launches its task child, and stalls before persisting; run B then reads `ddflow next`, finds item 102 still unleased, claims it (the lease never fires, because A and B claimed disjoint items), and persists the newer wave position into `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; when A's child merges 101, A persists its older wave position over B's. A later compaction or restart of run B loads A's stale position and loses track of 102's in-flight/merged status. The lease therefore does not make the "never written by two runs" claim true, and the earlier confirmed defect (persistence keyed only by scope, with no run/invocation id or slot lock) still stands at this new wording; the change also gives no instruction telling a second run to stop when its claims fail, while rule 5 says stop happens only on DONE or a question, so the losing run keeps driving and keeps writing the shared slot.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36-37 (and the identical text at ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:35-36)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten VS Code background loop still gives the orchestrating request a direct claim step: “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge”. That contradicts the immediately preceding sentence, which says the fan-out dispatches each ready item to a window/terminal agent that “claims its OWN item”. Given one ready item `101`, a background VS Code surface following this paragraph fans `101` to a terminal agent (which will claim `101`) and then follows the “claim” instruction itself; ddflow’s exclusive lease then refuses one of the two claims, so either the child cannot start or the background contends, and the wave can stall or skip that item. The delta should say the dispatched processes claim/gate/merge while the background only waits and re-reads. The same text is in `docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The added “enforcement” does not make the persistence slot single-writer. ddflow’s claim lease is item-scoped — the text itself says “those items already leased” — not a run/scope mutex. Given a scope with two ready items 101 and 102, run A can claim 101 and pause before saving, while run B (`/ddflow-wave bugs`) starts, claims 102, and saves `orchestrator_wave:bugs`; then A saves its older read over B’s slot. A later compaction/restart resumes from whichever write landed last, not necessarily the newest wave. This is the previous persistence-overwrite defect still present; the claim-lease fix does not answer it because it only stops duplicate per-item claims, not concurrent same-scope runs writing the same memory key.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36 (rule 4) and ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:36 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: The empty-scope stop test is `empty scope (no ready, no held/blocked, none in flight)`, but the new dispatch model tells the background surface to fan each ready item WITHOUT claiming it (lines 13-14) and then re-read only `ddflow next --json`. `ddflow next` does not list an item that has been claimed and is still being implemented; the matching Kilo loop in this same change requires a separate “no item you claimed is still in flight” test for exactly that reason. Because the vscode surface did not claim the items and is given no instruction to wait for or track the spawned window/terminal agents, it cannot evaluate “none in flight.” Concrete input: ready items 101 and 102 are fanned to two agents; 102 merges first. The surface re-reads `ddflow next --json` and sees no ready and no held/blocked (101 is claimed/unreported). It can declare the scope empty and stop/hand off while 101 is still being implemented, so the loop stops before all in-flight work has finished.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:16 (same text in docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md)

chunk_findings.detail: The handoff instruction still says to output `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence`, with underscores. The actual commands used throughout ddflow and earlier in this same delta are `ddflow next` and `ddflow cadence` (space-separated). An agent following this literally outputs `ddflow_next`, which is not a valid command, so the handoff is broken.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:19 (same text in docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md)

chunk_findings.detail: The new ownership rule persists “your own agent/session id” and tells the agent to stop if, on resume, the stored id is not the current one, but it never clears the slot on a normal stop or checks whether the stored owner is still alive. This makes a completed or crashed run permanently own the scope. For example, run A starts `/ddflow-wave bugs`, saves session id `s1`, then crashes; a later Kilo session starts as `s2`, loads `orchestrator_wave:bugs`, sees `s1 != s2`, and follows rule 4 by stopping instead of resuming or starting, even though no run owns the scope. The same text is shipped in `.kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md`, so the emitted agent inherits the failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:33

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope stop defines completion as `ddflow next` reporting “no ready and no held/blocked” and then asserts “an in-flight item is held by its lease.” That assertion is not how the corrected wave loop semantics work: a claimed/in-flight item is not reported as `held`/`blocked` by `ddflow next`, which is why the Kilo wave rule requires a separate “no item you claimed is still in flight” check. Given a scope with one ready item `101`, the background request fans `101` to a terminal/window agent, that agent claims it and is still implementing it. A re-read of `ddflow next --json` now returns no ready and no held/blocked items, so this text tells the VS Code driver that the scope is empty and the request may stop and print the handoff while `101` is still in flight, prematurely ending the wave and leaving no driver waiting for the merge/park.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The new ownership token is checked only “On resume, if the stored id is not yours,” not when a fresh `/ddflow-wave` run starts. A brand-new run never reads the existing `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` before claiming or saving, so two concurrent same-scope runs can still overwrite each other’s wave position. Concrete interleaving: an operator launches `/ddflow-wave bugs` from two terminals. Run A saves wave 10 with id A; run B starts fresh, sees no resume condition, claims items, and saves wave 12 with id B, overwriting A. Run A then saves wave 11 over B. A later compaction or restart resumes from whichever write landed last, potentially re-claiming or skipping items. The stated “one `/ddflow-wave` run per scope at a time” is therefore still not enforced for concurrent fresh starts.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32-36 (rule 4; same text in ddflow/templates/agents/kilo/ddflow-orchestrator.md:31-35)

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope condition asserts that “an in-flight item is held by its lease,” so it defines empty solely as `ddflow next` reporting no ready and no held/blocked. But this VS Code driver has the background surface fan each ready item to a child process that claims its own item, and the surface keeps no separate record of which children are still implementing. `ddflow next` after a claim does not show the claimed, still-in-flight item as held/blocked — the Kilo loop in this same change had to add an explicit “no item you claimed is still in flight” check for exactly that reason. Concrete failure: with one ready item `101`, the surface fans `101` to a terminal agent, which claims it and starts the gates/merge; the surface re-reads `ddflow next`, sees no ready and no held/blocked, and, following this line, treats the scope as empty and stops/hands off before `101` completes. The stop condition must test for no fanned/claimed item still in flight, not infer that state from `ddflow next`’s held/blocked categories.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten stop condition defines completion as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited … and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” but it no longer requires that there be no held or blocked items. Given a VS Code background wave on a scope with ready item `101` and blocked item `102` (for example, `102` waiting on an unmet dependency), the driver fans `101`; after `101` merges and its child exits, `ddflow next --json` reports no ready items. Following line 17 literally, the driver treats that as the empty scope and stops, even though `102` remains blocked and the scope is not DONE. The corrected wave loop requires no ready, held, blocked, or in-flight items before stopping, so this delta can abandon remaining work.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The new VS Code wave stop condition defines completion as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited (merged or parked) and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” dropping the previous “no held/blocked” part of the empty-scope test. Since `ddflow next` only reports ready work, a scope with no ready or in-flight items but one blocked item (for example, an item waiting on an unmet dependency) satisfies this literal rule, so a background VS Code driver can stop and treat the scope as complete while blocked work remains; the corrected wave DONE test used elsewhere in this change requires no held or blocked items left.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:18

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten vscode empty-scope stop condition now says to stop when all dispatched windows/terminals have exited and `ddflow next` reports “nothing ready,” but it no longer requires `ddflow next` to report no held/blocked items. Given a scope whose only remaining work is a held or blocked item (for example an item `ddflow park`ed waiting on a long gate, or blocked on an unmet dependency), `ddflow next --json` reports that item as held/blocked rather than ready, and no dispatched window is running; an agent following this text treats the scope as empty and stops, leaving the held/blocked item unprocessed. The previous wording explicitly included “no ready and no held/blocked”; the new wording drops the held/blocked half of the completion test.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17

chunk_findings.detail: The new empty-scope stop condition is defined as “each dispatched window/terminal has exited (merged or parked) and `ddflow next` reports nothing ready,” but it omits held/blocked items. Concrete input: a scope has one held or blocked item and no ready items, and all previously dispatched windows/terminals have exited. `ddflow next` reports nothing ready, so an agent following this line stops the wave, leaving that held/blocked item unprocessed. The loop’s empty-scope condition must be no ready and no held/blocked items (plus no in-flight), as the rest of this change requires.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:17-18

chunk_findings.detail: The background orchestrator is first told to “fan each ready item to one window/terminal agent each (the dispatched process claims its OWN item)”, then in the same paragraph is told “Within one request keep going — claim, run the gates, merge”. Concrete input: one ready item 101; the orchestrator fans 101 to a child that claims it, then following the later “claim” instruction attempts to claim 101 itself. ddflow’s exclusive lease refuses that duplicate claim, so the wave stalls or errors. The orchestrating request must not claim an item it has already handed to a self-claiming child.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/vscode.md:19

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten background-loop instruction tells the VS Code surface to end the request by printing `ddflow_next` and `ddflow_cadence`. An agent following this emitted delta literally prints invalid command names, so the stated handoff/restart point is not a valid ddflow command and the wave handoff is broken.

The earlier fix rejects a missing `loop` key by checking `table.get("loop") is None`, but an explicit `[orchestration] loop = ""` is not `None`, so that guard does not fire; then the added `_validate_section` check is `if orch and orch.loop:`, which skips `_membership` because `""` is falsy. Given a descriptor such as `[orchestration]
loop = ""` (or `[orchestration]
dispatch = "task"
loop = ""`), validation passes and the emitted `Orchestration` has `loop=""`, which is not in `ORCHESTRATION_LOOPS` and therefore emits a wave driver with no valid background loop primitive.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:254-256

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding #4 still stands in this emitted copy. The text records the desired outcome — “a compaction or restart resumes AT the wave, never before it” — but it does not give the restarted run an instruction to load `orchestrator_wave:<scope>` before starting. Concrete failure: the orchestrator claims item A and launches a `task` child, then a compaction/restart occurs before the merge. The new run starts at rule 1, calls `ddflow next --json` in rule 2, and never reads the saved slot. If `ddflow next` exits 2 and shows no held/blocked items, rule 2 declares the scope DONE while A is still being implemented, because the slot that proves A was claimed-but-not-merged was never consulted. The probe that refuted #4 equated the outcome statement with a read-back action, but the emitted rules contain no such action.
chunk_findings.title: .kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md:32 (rule 4)

chunk_findings.detail: For any harness whose descriptor declares `[subagents].files` (Kilo does in this change), `_write_harness_files` calls `_write_command(repo, dst, templates / src, "agents")`. The existing `_write_command` used for the `AGENT_COMMANDS` path takes only `(repo, dst, src)` and this diff does not widen its signature, so the first non-empty `AGENT_SUBAGENTS` entry raises `TypeError: _write_command() takes 3 positional arguments but 4 were given` while building the actions list. Adoption aborts before any subagent file is written, so the emitted `.kilo/agent/ddflow-orchestrator.md` is never produced.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt/_commands.py:_write_harness_files

chunk_findings.detail: The added guard `if orch and orch.loop:` skips `_membership` for any falsey `loop` value. Descriptor input `[orchestration]` with `loop = ""` yields a present, non-`None` key, so the earlier missing-loop guard added for the confirmed no-key defect does not fire; `orch.loop` is then false and the membership check is never called. The record is accepted with `loop=""`, which is not one of `ORCHESTRATION_LOOPS`, allowing a malformed orchestration record to be built and emitted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessv2.py:_validate_section (new `orchestration.loop` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The new opencode loop tells the orchestrator to claim every ready item, fan the claimed items to sub-agents, and stop “when the scope is empty,” but it never requires waiting for all fanned sub-agents to exit before judging the scope empty. Given `ddflow next --json` returning items A and B: the orchestrator claims both and dispatches one sub-agent each; A merges quickly. On that merge the orchestrator re-reads `next`; B is still claimed/in-flight, so `next` reports no ready/held/blocked. The bullet’s only emptiness condition is “scope is empty,” so the orchestrator can stop and orphan B. The intended done test includes “no item you claimed is still in-flight” (the vscode delta spells it out as “until each dispatched window/terminal has exited”), and this opencode delta omits that condition.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/opencode.md item 1

chunk_findings.detail: The new `[orchestration]` section in `claude.toml` (and equivalently in `kilo.toml`, `opencode.toml`, and `vscode.toml`) introduces harness configuration facts without a corresponding update to the `[verified]` sources or date. Under rule `[r-agent-parity]`, "a fact is unverified until a probe or source is recorded", and adding unverified capability or loop facts without a source or verification timestamp leaves the parity state non-compliant.

chunk_findings.detail: `tier_notes` decides whether to suppress the model-tier hint by looking only at `evidence["independence_tier"]` on reviewer gate records; it does not check whether those records correspond to reviews that actually passed/were available. For example, if an item has `critic` recorded as `passed=True` with `evidence={"model": "claude-haiku", "independence_tier": "model"}` and `roborev` recorded as `passed=False` with `evidence={"model": "gpt-4", "independence_tier": "family"}`, the guard `any(r.evidence.get("independence_tier") == "family")` returns true and `tier_notes` returns `[]`. `ddflow complete`/gate status then omits the required model-tier hint even though the best tier among passing reviewers is `model`. The intent says the gate tier is the best tier among passing reviewers, and a review that could not run/failed is unavailable, not a cross-family review.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py:`tier_notes`

chunk_findings.detail: The exact-text assertion locks the tier-model hint to the placeholder form `` `ddflow review --reviewer <name>` `` rather than naming the reviewer(s) that are actually configured. D-reviewer-independence-soft requires complete/gate status to name the exact way to get a family review, including which reviewers are configured, and r-tell-dont-discover requires the tool to tell the user instead of making them discover the reviewer name. Given a project whose only configured cross-family reviewer is `roborev`, the enforced note still tells the user to run `ddflow review --reviewer <name>`, leaving the actual name (`roborev`) to be discovered; the previous exact-text fix does not answer this because the exact text it asserts itself omits the configured reviewer names.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_reviewer_independence_soft.py:98 (`test_tier_notes_are_neutral_and_once`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `if level == "off": return "off", ...` branch still runs before `state.items.get(item_id)` or any reviewer inspection. With `[agent].reviewer_independence = "off"` (or legacy `reviewer_family_must_differ=false`) and a project whose only reachable reviewer model is the author's own model, this function returns tier `"off"`; the gate records that as an acceptable independence tier and passes. That violates the operator clarification D-reviewer-independence-soft-why(e): the hard floor stays — the author's own model never counts and with only one model reachable the gate is recorded unavailable, never passed. The earlier refutation's probes cover the floor at model/family, not off, so this branch still stands.
